lead: Semiconductor photodevices turn light into an electrical signal. A photodiode gives a current, a phototransistor gives a larger current, a photovoltaic cell gives a voltage, and a photoconductive cell changes resistance. These devices are cheap, small and fast, so they appear in light meters, remote controls, solar panels, safety curtains and laboratory instruments. A spectrophotometer uses them to measure how much light a solution absorbs; from that absorption it finds concentration. This chapter explains each device, compares them, and then shows the source, monochromator, sample and detector path of a spectrophotometer with the Beer-Lambert law.
prereq: You need: photoelectric transducers and fibre sensors and a basic picture of a semiconductor pn junction.

sections.h3: Photodiode, phototransistor, photovoltaic and photoconductive cells

blocks.text: A photodiode is a reverse-biased pn junction. Light absorbed in the depletion region creates electron-hole pairs. The electric field sweeps electrons to the n side and holes to the p side, so an external circuit sees a photocurrent. Reverse bias widens the depletion layer, lowers junction capacitance and makes the response faster. The photocurrent is I<sub>p</sub> = R P, where I<sub>p</sub> is photocurrent in A, P is incident optical power in W, and R is responsivity in A/W. Responsivity depends on wavelength and on the semiconductor.

blocks.where: I<sub>p</sub> is photocurrent in A; R is responsivity in A/W; P is incident optical power in W.

blocks.text: Dark current I<sub>d</sub> is the small reverse current with no light. It adds an offset and shot noise. A PIN photodiode puts an intrinsic layer between p and n. The thicker absorption layer raises responsivity and keeps capacitance low. An avalanche photodiode uses a high field to create impact ionization and internal gain, but it needs a higher bias and adds excess noise.

items: Phototransistor: a photodiode drives the base of a transistor, so the current is multiplied by current gain β. It is more sensitive but slower than a photodiode.
Photovoltaic cell: an unbiased pn junction. Light produces a forward voltage and can deliver power to a load; it is a solar cell, not a linear light sensor.
Photoconductive cell or LDR: light lowers the resistance of a semiconductor film, often CdS. It is cheap and simple but slow, nonlinear and has memory effects.

blocks.text: Spectral response is the device output plotted against wavelength λ. The band gap sets the long-wavelength limit: a photon with energy hν below the band gap is not absorbed, where h is Planck constant and ν is optical frequency. Silicon peaks in the near infrared near 850–900 nm; indium gallium arsenide works near 1300–1550 nm for fibre links; cadmium sulphide responds in the visible. Always state the wavelength when you quote responsivity.

A spectrophotometer measures absorption at one chosen wavelength. A source gives white light: tungsten lamp for visible, deuterium lamp for ultraviolet, or an LED for a fixed wavelength. A monochromator uses a prism or diffraction grating to pass a narrow band. The beam passes through a cuvette of path length l and reaches a detector such as a photodiode, phototransistor or photomultiplier tube. The readout compares the sample with a blank.

items: Set the wavelength and zero the instrument with a blank cuvette.
Compute transmittance T = I / I₀ and absorbance A = −log₁₀ T.
Use A = ε c l to find concentration c when ε and l are known.

blocks.where: T is transmittance, dimensionless; I is transmitted light intensity; I₀ is incident or blank light intensity.
A is absorbance, dimensionless; T is transmittance; I and I₀ are transmitted and incident intensities.
A is absorbance; ε is molar absorptivity in L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹; c is concentration in mol/L; l is path length in cm.

blocks.text: Absorbance is logarithmic, so it adds when samples add. A = 0.30 means I/I₀ = 10⁻⁰·³⁰ = 0.50, so half the light is transmitted. The linear range is limited: too high c gives A above about 2, and stray light and detector nonlinearity bend the curve. Use a dilution or a shorter cell. Applications include dyes and inks, protein assays, nitrate and phosphate in water, haemoglobin in clinical chemistry, drug dissolution and HPLC detection.

figure.caption: White light is reduced to one wavelength, passes through the sample, and the detector current becomes an absorbance reading. Notice that the sample changes only the light that reaches the detector.

spec.title: Spectrophotometer path
spec.aria: A light source passes through a monochromator and sample, and a detector plus readout gives absorbance at the chosen wavelength.

examples.question: A spectrophotometer reads absorbance A = 0.30 in a 1.00 cm cell. The molar absorptivity at that wavelength is 1500 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. Find the concentration in mol/L.
steps: Write the Beer-Lambert law: A = ε c l.
List the known values: A = 0.30, ε = 1500 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, l = 1.00 cm.
Rearrange for concentration: c = A / (ε l).
Compute the denominator: ε l = 1500 × 1.00 = 1500 L mol⁻¹.
examples.check:
A = 0.30
epsilon = 1500
l = 1.00
c = A / (epsilon * l)
print(c)

traps: Absorbance is logarithmic. Doubling concentration doubles A only inside the linear range; it does not double transmittance.
A = ε c l needs c in mol/L and l in cm. Convert a path length given in mm or a concentration given in mmol/L before dividing.
Dark current is not a light signal. It adds an offset, so zero or subtract it correctly and do not treat it as absorbance.
Responsivity in A/W is wavelength dependent. A value quoted at 850 nm cannot be used at 1550 nm without a new calibration.
An LDR is slow and nonlinear; a photovoltaic cell is a power source. Neither is a good choice for fast, precise spectrophotometry.

quiz.q: Define responsivity of a photodiode and give its unit.
quiz.a: Responsivity is photocurrent divided by incident optical power, R = I_p / P. Its unit is A/W.

quiz.q: Why does reverse bias make a photodiode faster?
quiz.a: Reverse bias widens the depletion region and raises the electric field. The wider region lowers junction capacitance, and the stronger field sweeps carriers out quickly, so the response is faster.

quiz.q: A photodiode has responsivity R = 0.50 A/W at 850 nm. The incident optical power is 20 µW. Find the photocurrent.
Why is a phototransistor more sensitive but slower than a photodiode?
quiz.a: The photodiode current drives the transistor base, so the output is multiplied by current gain β. This gives more sensitivity. The extra junction capacitance and stored charge make the response slower.

quiz.q: A sample gives transmittance T = 0.20 in a 1.00 cm cell. The molar absorptivity is 2500 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. Find A and c.
Why does the Beer-Lambert plot bend at high concentration?
quiz.a: At high absorbance, stray light and detector nonlinearity become a large fraction of the signal. The sample may also change its refractive index or chemistry. These effects break the simple A = ε c l relation, so the solution must be diluted or a shorter cell used.

quiz.q: Name two types of photodiode used for light detection.
quiz.a: PIN photodiode and avalanche photodiode. A simple pn photodiode is also used.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern instruments use array detectors and CCDs to capture a whole spectrum at once. Photodiode arrays with transimpedance amplifiers reach high speed and low noise. In research, silicon photomultipliers and avalanche arrays count single photons. Search next for transimpedance amplifier design, spectrophotometer linearity and stray light, and Beer-Lambert deviations.
